name: Zoe Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am the principal organist for a cathedral choir, teach five keyboard pupils and record hymn guides for nearby congregations. My music master’s and years leading singers make me a strong player, but the salary is ordinary for a musician. I like hearing the choir find a clear pitch before I touch the next chord.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does the work meet home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a carpenter with regular site work, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have five months of expenses saved and some other organ posts nearby. I still need to arrange every evening rehearsal around pickup and supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that a quicker service calendar is welcome if paid rehearsal hours stay on it. The organist must still hear a singer lose the pitch and give it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cathedral contract and my partner’s site pay cover our mortgage, with five months saved. An ordinary cancelled wedding fee still matters, but I do not expect the mild AI change to remove my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid cathedral services and five keyboard pupils this season. I have never used an AI tool and would check the paper service rota; before wedding season I would ask for a written cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household in this picture. We can absorb one missed wedding without changing the children’s plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a wedding date change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family moved a ceremony last spring after I had practised the music. I was paid for the new day but not the lost preparation, so the next contract needs a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a pupil about practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell pupils to listen before they press a key. An organ can fill a room and still miss the person who needs the tune.

I would request a **written wedding cancellation fee**.
think: Our **five-month reserve** and steady site pay make one lost wedding manageable.
The **cathedral contract** remains paid under this mild change.
do: Keep **paid cathedral services** and five keyboard pupils this season.
Request a **written cancellation fee** before wedding season.
feel: I feel **calm** because current work and savings cover one missed fee.
S0.quote: An organ can fill a room and still miss the person who needs the tune.
fieldNote: Her **senior organ skill** earns typical pay, with five months saved and another regular household wage.
She has **never used AI** and checks service dates on paper.

steps.text: Keep paid cathedral services and five keyboard pupils this season
Request written wedding cancellation fee before next wedding season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir committee that software may make hymn guides and calendars cheaply. I would ask for the rehearsal rate and recording reuse fee in the next written contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide recordings bring about a fifth of my own pay, so fewer orders would reduce what we put aside. The cathedral still needs live music, but I cannot treat its next season as signed yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask the choir committee for a paid season in writing and keep the five pupils. In the first year, if guide orders fall, I would stop hiring the outside recording room on unused days and apply for a nearby posted paid organ seat only if the service times fit pickup and written net pay after travel beats lost fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a lasting cut to my own recording pay. Five months saved lets me seek a paid organ seat; savings do not replace lost hymn-guide fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you make the guides with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool and would rather play the guide myself. I would not send a pupil’s singing to a service I do not understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is any nearby organ seat suitable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would only audition for a posted paid chair that calls for my experience. My partner cannot promise every evening pickup on a carpenter’s site schedule.

I would remind the committee that **live organ work** remains paid work.
think: Guide recordings bring **one fifth** of my own income and help us build the mortgage reserve.
The next **cathedral season** is not signed yet, even if live organ work remains wanted.
do: Request a **written paid season** from the committee this month.
Stop **unused room hire** if guide orders fall; seek posted paid organ seat with replacement net-after-travel pay and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible sustained recording losses.
S1.quote: Five months saved lets me seek a paid organ seat; savings do not replace lost hymn-guide fees.
fieldNote: She resists **AI tool use** but responds to threatened recording pay with written terms and cost control.
A different **organ seat** needs a posted paid opening, suitable experience, better net travel pay and pickup fit.

steps.text: Keep five keyboard pupils while requesting written paid cathedral season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that thinking AGI by 2028 could make hymn guides almost at once. Hands-on organ-playing robots follow around 2031, three years later, and our service rota needs written pay now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the guide orders to end in 2028, taking a fifth of my own earnings. The cathedral may also shorten paid rehearsals, but I do not know that yet; our five-month reserve gives us time to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would count guide invoices and request a signed service calendar. In the first year after 2028, if guide orders stop and paid rehearsals fall, I would apply for an advertised school keyboard post only if my music master’s and any required licence qualify, its written net pay after travel and childcare beats the lost fees and school pickup works; I would keep cathedral services and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the expected guide loss, though I still have paid services and a few nearby options. I would be alarmed if rehearsals also fell sharply, but that is a possibility rather than my forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a teaching licence first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the posted school requirements before buying a course. Our savings are for the mortgage and a real transition, not a guessed qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could cover a school interview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can take one pickup if the site foreman releases him. A school timetable needs reliable child pickup every week, not one carpenter’s favour.

I would seek **signed service pay** before auditioning elsewhere.
think: I expect **hymn-guide fees** to end in 2028, removing a fifth of my music income.

do: Count **guide invoices** and request signed cathedral dates now.
Seek **posted school work** after 2028 only if guides and rehearsals fall, qualified, written net pay beats losses and pickup fits.
Keep **services and pupils** until a suitable written school offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording loss with some search time.
S2.quote: A school timetable needs reliable child pickup every week, not one carpenter’s favour.
fieldNote: The expected **2028 guide loss** removes a fifth of her pay before 2031 organ-playing robots arrive.
A school move needs **posted eligibility**, written net pay after travel/childcare, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Seek eligible posted school role if 2028 guides and rehearsals fall; replacement written net-after-travel/childcare, pickup
Keep paid cathedral services and pupils until suitable written school offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that five years until AGI by 2031 gives us time to teach families what live accompaniment sounds like. Robots able to play the organ follow around 2034, after the guide market changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide fees could still end in 2031. A separate beginner organ group might replace some pay, but four parents saying yes is not four parents paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would ask a separate parish hall for an available Saturday room after our children’s pickup. I would run a four-week beginner organ class only if six families prepay enough to cover hall hire, my teaching and preparation, and the hall checks the loan keyboards and power leads or families bring safe instruments; in the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only if six still prepay those costs, the room remains available after pickup and instruments stay safe. I would keep the cathedral and pupils while paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until a class pays my time. Five years before AGI lets me test a paid organ class without spending the mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is unsafe about a loan keyboard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall must check the power lead and stand before a child uses it. If it cannot, families bring sound instruments or I cancel the class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four families pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees cannot cover hall hire and my preparation. I would refund them and keep the five pupils I already teach.

Keep **cathedral services** and five pupils while paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to learn a trade and ask for paid work. Organ-playing robots arrive around 2039, three years after the guide market changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still have a cathedral contract, but a mortgage is due every month until then. Five months saved means we can make a careful plan without claiming the future services are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would save half of each extra paid wedding fee after food and mortgage until our reserve reaches six months. Through the decade I would run the separate organ class only with six family prepayments covering hall, teaching and preparation, safe instruments and a room after pickup; in the first year after 2036 I would seek a posted school keyboard job only if cathedral pay falls, the school accepts my qualifications and written net pay after travel and childcare replaces lost fees. I would keep cathedral work and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the distant contract, with current services paid. A decade gives us time to protect a reserve without gambling on an empty classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if wedding fees stop before six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save only spare paid lesson fees after bills and keep four months of expenses untouched. A wedding inquiry is not a paid invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a school title for less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would need a posted role and a written net wage that covers the missing cathedral money and pickup. I would not give notice for a pleasant interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the hymn guides could stop before the cathedral signs its next paid season. Signed service dates, recording reuse terms and a real school keyboard vacancy with accepted credentials, written net pay and covered pickup would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether anyone paid the organist to prepare the hymn before the wedding. A wedding march is not free just because the family hears it once.

headlineQuote: A wedding march is not free just because the family hears it once.
portrait: At **43**, Zoe is a senior cathedral organist with a music master’s and strong skill, teaching five pupils and recording hymn guides.
Her **typical pay**, carpenter partner, two children, mortgage and five-month reserve support careful choices.
She **never uses AI** and prefers written service rates, paid preparation and direct playing.
She tests a **separate organ class** only with six prepayments covering hall and teaching, safe keyboards and pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end hymn-guide fees before the cathedral confirms paid service dates.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed cathedral dates**, reuse terms and a qualifying posted school job with written net pay and pickup would help.
